before: > "I know you're in there. I love you. You don't have to love me back or trust me yet. I can't promise that nothing painful will happen. Or that I'll always know what to do, or never react badly. But I can promise to tell you the truth and listen when you're angry. I'll make our life together safer where I can, and take the next step I can see to protect you. When I fail, I'll come back to make it right. You don't have to believe these words. Watch what I do."
after: Only say the "I love you" part if you can feel it. If you don't feel the love yet, say you care (with the goodwill prayer from before). That's a first step. Or even before that, just promise your little one you won't be cruel to them on purpose.

next: Use “I love you” only when it is honest. Otherwise, use a sincere wish for wellbeing or a commitment to non-cruelty without pretending they feel the same.

Joel's standing rules: never call the inner child "the kid"; invent no facts about his life; banned: "doesn't get to decide" and its family, "Fine,"/"Good,"/"Great," as a clause, wry humor. No emojis from the writers.

I don't think faking love is a good idea because that's not an action that speaks for itself, it's a feeling that we have to trust is there." Acts can be practiced before they feel natural; love is felt. Never word a condition as a question of the reader's sincerity.
Joel, 2026-10-01 20:51, on P5: "it sounds too biased towards adulting"; "If they show up to have some innocent fun, don't \"put them in their place\" as the adult." Joel, 2026-10-02 00:16, on the guide's caution that a comfort object isn't an oracle: "I don't think people will be confusing the stuffed animal with an oracle." A caution the reader doesn't need gets cut, not replaced with a vaguer one.
